---
title: "Labeling, stigma & system contact"
toc: true
---

## Motivation (stylized facts)
::: {.callout-note title="Stylized facts this mechanism aims to match"}
- System contact (arrest, conviction, incarceration) can change future outcomes beyond the immediate punishment.
- Stigma can alter employment, schooling, social ties, and incentives.
:::

---

## Mechanism (core idea)
Labeling theories emphasize that formal control can produce **secondary effects**:
- stigma changes opportunities (labor-market access, housing),
- social identity and peer grouping can shift,
- repeated contact can become self-reinforcing.

In a theory-first framework, stigma is modeled as a **state** that affects payoffs and constraints going forward.

---

## Canonical modeling primitives
- stigma state $z\in\{0,1\}$ (or continuous) that increases after system contact
- stigma reduces legal option $w(z)$ and/or increases network exposure to crime
- feedback loop: stigma → lower $w$ → higher crime incentives → more contact → more stigma

---

## Predictions (qualitative)
- Policies increasing detection/arrest can reduce crime short-run but may increase long-run crime if stigma harms future legal options.
- Diversion programs and record-sealing can improve long-run outcomes by weakening the stigma transition.
- The effect depends on who is marginally affected: high-risk vs low-risk populations.

---

## What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Empirical work often tries to separate:
- selection into system contact vs causal impact of contact on later employment/offending,
- short-run deterrence/incapacitation vs long-run stigma effects.

---

## Later-on analysis (model links)
- Fits naturally inside life-course dynamics and dynamic choice.
- Links to courts/corrections: sentencing policies determine stigma transitions.
- Provides a theory channel for observed persistence beyond stable “types.”
